subject: English
description: Common phrasal verbs — meaning, in-context use, often-confused pairs

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of 'put off' in: 'Due to rain, the meeting was PUT OFF until next week.'

options.option_text: Cancelled completely
Postponed / deferred
Approved
Disturbed

questions.explanation: PUT OFF — postpone, defer to a later date. Distinguish from CALL OFF — cancel entirely. Other 'put-' phrasals: PUT UP WITH (tolerate), PUT DOWN (insult / criticise), PUT ASIDE (save / ignore), PUT FORWARD (propose), PUT ON (wear), PUT OUT (extinguish a fire / publish), PUT THROUGH (connect a phone call).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Pick the meaning of 'GIVE IN' in: 'After hours of arguing, he finally GAVE IN.'

options.option_text: Distributed something
Surrendered / yielded
Donated to charity
Replied

questions.explanation: GIVE IN — surrender / yield to pressure. Confusing 'give-' phrasals: GIVE UP (abandon, stop trying), GIVE AWAY (donate, reveal a secret), GIVE OFF (emit — heat, smell), GIVE OUT (distribute / run out), GIVE BACK (return). Each carries a specific meaning — context decides which fits.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in: 'He always _____ his elder brother.'

options.option_text: looks down on
looks up to (= respects, admires)
looks into
looks after

questions.explanation: LOOKS UP TO — respects, admires, takes as a role model. Opposite: LOOKS DOWN ON — despises, regards with contempt. Other 'look-' phrasals: LOOK INTO (investigate), LOOK AFTER (take care of), LOOK FOR (search), LOOK FORWARD TO (anticipate eagerly), LOOK OUT (be careful), LOOK OVER (examine briefly), LOOK BACK (recall the past), LOOK ON (watch passively).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the meaning of 'CARRY OUT' in: 'The scientists CARRIED OUT a series of experiments.'

options.option_text: Carried physically away
Conducted / performed / executed
Cancelled
Failed

questions.explanation: CARRY OUT — perform, execute (a task, plan, experiment, instruction). 'Carry out a survey / an attack / orders'. Other 'carry-' phrasals: CARRY ON (continue, persist), CARRY OFF (succeed at something difficult), CARRY OVER (transfer to next period — accounting), CARRY AWAY (overwhelmed with emotion, e.g., 'got carried away'). Don't confuse 'carry out' (do it) with 'cart away' (physical removal).

questions.stem: Match phrasal verb to meaning — which pairing is INCORRECT?

options.option_text: Break down — collapse / stop functioning
Break out — escape / start suddenly
Break in — boast about something
Break up — end a relationship / disperse

questions.explanation: BREAK IN means to enter forcibly (e.g., burglary) OR to interrupt a conversation. NOT 'boast'. Boasting is BOAST ABOUT or BLOW (one's own) TRUMPET. Phrasal-verb traps are common in SSC/Bank papers — the same verb + different particles can give very different meanings: BREAK DOWN (stop functioning), BREAK OUT (escape / start), BREAK IN (intrude), BREAK UP (separate), BREAK INTO (enter forcefully), BREAK OFF (terminate), BREAK THROUGH (achieve a major advance).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Pick the phrasal verb meaning 'to invent (a story / excuse)':

options.option_text: make up
make over
make for
make off

questions.explanation: MAKE UP — many meanings depending on context: (1) invent (a story, excuse) — 'he made up that excuse'; (2) constitute (make up the team); (3) cosmetics; (4) reconcile after a quarrel ('we made up'). MAKE OVER — transfer / give a makeover. MAKE FOR — head towards. MAKE OFF (WITH) — flee with stolen goods. MAKE OUT — succeed in seeing/hearing OR understand OR fare.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the phrasal verb meaning 'to RAISE / nurture (a child)':

options.option_text: bring out
bring up
bring about
bring down

questions.explanation: BRING UP — to rear / raise a child to adulthood. Also: introduce a topic in conversation ('don't bring up politics at dinner'). Other 'bring-' phrasals: BRING ABOUT — cause to happen; BRING OUT — publish, release; BRING DOWN — lower / reduce / overthrow government; BRING IN — earn (income), introduce (a law); BRING FORWARD — advance a date. Many phrasal verbs are CONTEXT-driven; sentence frame determines the meaning.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: In 'The management decided to LOOK INTO the allegations of fund misappropriation', what does 'LOOK INTO' mean?

options.option_text: To deliberately ignore a complaint or allegation
To investigate or examine a matter carefully
To view something at a single, quick glance
To look inside a physical object or enclosure

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'Look into' means to investigate or inquire into something in depth. Option A is the classic trap — 'overlook' means to ignore, not 'look into'. Option C treats the phrase literally as a physical act of peering inside something, which is incorrect in this figurative context.

questions.stem: In 'While searching through the old case files, the officer CAME ACROSS a crucial piece of evidence', what does 'CAME ACROSS' mean?

options.option_text: To deliver a convincing impression to an audience
To find something by chance or accidentally
To cross a road or a boundary with great care
To visit someone at their home or workplace

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'Come across' = to encounter or find something unexpectedly. Option A is a plausible distractor — 'come across well' means to make a good impression, but the context here involves finding something, not creating an impression. Option C is a literal misreading of the words.

questions.stem: In 'Despite his elaborate alibi, the senior investigator SAW THROUGH his pretence immediately', what does 'SAW THROUGH' mean?

options.option_text: To complete a difficult task or project to its end
To observe something via a transparent glass surface
To detect a deception or false pretence with clarity
To support someone throughout a challenging situation

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'See through' = to perceive the true nature of a deception; not be fooled. Option A is the most dangerous trap — 'see something through' (with an object between) means to complete it, but structurally and contextually it differs. Option D describes 'see someone through' (support), a distinct idiomatic use.

questions.stem: Which phrasal verb correctly fills the blank in 'The fire brigade arrived in time and managed to _____ the blaze before it reached the storage unit'?

options.option_text: put out — meaning to extinguish or stop burning
put off — meaning to postpone or delay an event
put down — meaning to place on a hard flat surface
put up — meaning to erect or display something

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'Put out' means to extinguish a fire. Options B, C, D all use 'put + particle' structures that fit the same sentence frame superficially, making them attractive traps — 'put off' means postpone, 'put down' means place or suppress, and 'put up' means erect or accommodate, none of which collocate meaningfully with 'a blaze'.

questions.stem: In 'When her primary source of income dried up, she had to FALL BACK ON her savings to meet daily expenses', what does 'FALL BACK ON' mean?

options.option_text: To physically lose balance and stumble backwards
To reconsider or reverse a decision made earlier
To reduce one's involvement or participation slowly
To rely on something kept in reserve as a backup

questions.explanation: D is correct: 'Fall back on' = to use a reserve resource or option when the primary one fails. Option B is a common mix-up with 'go back on' (to break a promise or commitment). Option C sounds plausible but actually describes 'pull back from'. Option A is a purely literal misreading of the words.

questions.stem: In 'Against considerable odds, the young diplomat managed to BRING OFF a landmark trade agreement in just three rounds of talks', what does 'BRING OFF' mean?

options.option_text: To succeed in accomplishing something surprisingly hard
To present or formally introduce something to others
To withdraw from an agreed commitment before it ends
To transfer or delegate responsibility to another body

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'Bring off' = to succeed in doing something that was difficult or seemed unlikely — a less common phrasal verb often confused with 'pull off' (synonym) or 'bring about' (cause to happen). Option B resembles 'bring out' (launch/reveal); Option C fits 'back out of'; Option D fits 'hand over'. All are deliberate structural distractors.

questions.stem: In 'The new CEO managed to TURN AROUND the ailing division, but analysts doubt whether the recovery will HOLD UP under independent scrutiny', what do the two phrasal verbs mean RESPECTIVELY?

options.option_text: Reverse a deteriorating situation; remain valid or credible
Physically rotate the unit; withstand an external force
Announce a restructuring plan; delay or defer a review
Revert to a previous condition; increase in resilience

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'Turn around' = to reverse the declining performance of something; 'hold up' = to remain sound, valid, or credible when subjected to scrutiny. Option C is the most tempting distractor — in business journalism 'turn around' is often paired with announcements, but that is not its phrasal-verb meaning. Option D confuses 'turn around' with 'revert' and misreads 'hold up' as increase in strength.
